content.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given daily stock prices, find the maximum profit achievable with unlimited buy and sell transactions, where after selling, a 1-day cooldown must pass before buying again (and only one share can be held at a time).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","prices array"],["Output","Maximum achievable profit with the cooldown restriction"],["Key Insight","Track three states per day: currently holding a share, just sold (in cooldown), or resting (free to buy)"],["Constraints","Up to 5000 days"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Unlimited transactions with a cooldown restriction after selling\"","A finite-state DP: track a small number of possible states per day (holding, just sold, resting), each built from the previous day's states"]]}

blocks.text: At the end of any given day, exactly one of three states applies: currently HOLDING a share (bought at some point, not yet sold), just SOLD today (in the mandatory 1-day cooldown, cannot buy tomorrow), or RESTING (not holding, and free to buy). Each state's best achievable profit can be computed from yesterday's states: holding today either continues from yesterday's holding, or is a fresh buy from yesterday's resting state (never from just-sold, due to the cooldown); just-sold today comes from yesterday's holding plus today's price; resting today is the better of yesterday's resting or yesterday's just-sold (the cooldown day has passed).

blocks.title: Analogy: A Trader Who Must Rest One Day After Every Sale
blocks.text: Picture a trader tracking their best profit under three possible situations each day: currently holding stock, having JUST sold (forced to sit out tomorrow), or freely resting (able to buy). Each day's best profit in every situation is built directly from yesterday's best profits in the appropriate situations.

blocks.caption: Three states per day (holding, just sold, resting), each built from yesterday's states

blocks.text: Maximum profit = 3 (buy at price 1, sell at price 2, profit 1; cooldown one day; buy at price 0, sell at price 2, profit 2; total profit 3).
Maximum profit = 0 (a single day, no transaction possible).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: On any given day, being in the HOLDING state means either continuing to hold from yesterday, or freshly buying today (only possible if yesterday was RESTING, never right after a sale, due to cooldown).

Observation 2: Being in the JUST_SOLD state today means selling today, which requires having been HOLDING yesterday, adding today's price to yesterday's holding profit.

Observation 3: Being in the RESTING state today means NOT holding and NOT just having sold, so it takes the better of yesterday's RESTING or yesterday's JUST_SOLD (the cooldown from an even earlier sale has already passed).

Observation 4: The final answer is the better of ending in JUST_SOLD or RESTING (ending while still HOLDING would mean an unsold share, never optimal since prices are known in advance).
This leads to three rolling variables (hold, sold, rest), updated together each day from the previous day's values.
Recursively try buying, selling, or doing nothing on every day, tracking whether a cooldown is currently in effect, without memoization.
Why the code is written this way

items: Recursively trying every action per day directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same (day, holding, cooldown) states repeatedly across branches, costing exponential time; three rolling variables reuse yesterday's computed states directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to n) without memoization.
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: three rolling variables, updated once per day, compute the same answer using O(1) extra space and O(n) time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize hold = negative infinity (cannot be holding before any day passes), sold = 0, rest = 0. For each day's price: compute the new sold as the OLD hold plus today's price (selling today); update hold to the better of its own previous value (keep holding) or the OLD rest minus today's price (buy today); update rest to the better of its own previous value or the OLD sold (yesterday's cooldown has now passed). Careful: use the values from BEFORE this day's updates when computing each new state, since they all depend on YESTERDAY's values simultaneously. The final answer is the larger of sold and rest.
Use three rolling variables (hold, sold, rest), each day's new values computed from yesterday's values.

Carefully using each state's value from BEFORE the current day's updates (saving prevSold before overwriting it, and using the still-unmodified hold and rest for this day's sold and hold updates respectively) correctly ensures every day's three new states are built purely from YESTERDAY's states, exactly matching the intended recurrence; since holding profit starts at negative infinity, buying is naturally disallowed until a legitimate first purchase.

blocks.text: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown is a finite-state machine DP problem: a small fixed number of states per day, each built cleanly from yesterday's states.

items: Using an ALREADY-UPDATED state value (from earlier in the same day's update) instead of yesterday's value, corrupting the simultaneous update.
Forgetting the cooldown means buying can only happen from the RESTING state, never directly from JUST_SOLD.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "three states per day, each built purely from yesterday's states, carefully avoiding using an already-updated value" heads off the most common bug in this pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "unlimited transactions with a cooldown restriction", think: a finite-state DP tracking holding, just-sold, and resting states per day.

items: How would this change if there were also a transaction FEE per sale, in addition to (or instead of) the cooldown?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^n); the three-rolling-variable finite-state DP costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: finite-state machine dynamic programming with a small fixed number of states per day.
Core Idea: track holding, just-sold, and resting states, each day's values built from yesterday's values simultaneously.
Time: O(2^n) for the brute force, O(n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(1) extra for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: buying can only happen from the resting state, never directly after selling (the cooldown).
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately tricky medium-level DP problem.
One line memory trick: hold, sold, rest, each built from yesterday.
